subject: 배신의 특수성
title: Why betrayal is worse than mere harm
content: Being injured by an enemy is bad; being injured by somebody close is worse, and the difference is not merely a matter of feeling. Moral philosophy has reason to treat betrayal as a distinct category, since the wrong involves something beyond whatever damage was done. Consider what the betrayer had that a stranger lacks. Access, trust, and knowledge were extended to them precisely because they were expected not to use these things against the person who supplied them. Therefore the betrayal converts a gift into a weapon, and the very openness that made the relationship valuable becomes the means of the injury. A stranger who inflicted identical damage would have had to work considerably harder. A second element concerns what the act says. Ordinary wrongdoing treats somebody as an obstacle or a resource; betrayal treats them as somebody whose trust could be accepted and then discarded, which denies the standing that the relationship had established. This explains why victims frequently describe the discovery rather than the damage as the worst part, and why compensation so rarely settles anything. A third element concerns what is lost afterwards. The injured party must revise not only their view of one person but their confidence in their own judgment, since they were mistaken about somebody they knew well. That revision spreads, making later trust harder, so the harm continues to operate long after the original act. What follows for moral assessment is that betrayal cannot be measured by consequences alone. Two acts producing identical damage may differ enormously in gravity depending on the relation between the parties, and any theory that counts only outcomes will misdescribe the case. Justice here attends to what was given before the wrong occurred, which is exactly what the arithmetic of harm leaves out.

subject: 애도의 의미
title: What grief is for
content: Grief is painful, prolonged, and appears to accomplish nothing. It does not restore what was lost, it interferes with everything else, and a person might reasonably wish to be free of it. Yet almost nobody regards a person who felt nothing after a serious loss as fortunate, which suggests that grief carries a value the pain conceals. One account treats grief as the perception of a truth. Somebody mattered, they are gone, and the world is genuinely worse in a way that no adjustment can repair. On this reading the pain is not a malfunction but an accurate registration of what happened, and feeling nothing would mean failing to see something real. The person who grieves is not confused; they are correct. A second account attends to what grief does over time. The mourner had a life organised around somebody's presence — habits, plans, and expectations built on their being there — and grief is the slow work of dismantling and rebuilding that structure. Each fresh reminder is a place where the old arrangement fails, therefore the process cannot be hurried without leaving the structure unrepaired. This explains why grief comes in waves rather than declining smoothly. A third account concerns what the mourner learns about themselves. Loss reveals the shape of an attachment that was invisible while it functioned, so grieving is partly a discovery of what somebody meant. That knowledge is valuable even though its price is unbearable. What these accounts share is a refusal to treat grief as a disorder requiring correction. Support is appropriate and sometimes necessary, and yet the goal cannot be to remove the response, because the response is the form that love takes when its object is gone. A moral vocabulary that lacks room for that truth will describe mourners as failing when they are doing something demanding and right.

subject: 국경은 도덕적으로 무엇인가
title: What a border is, morally speaking
content: A line on the ground determines an enormous amount about a person's life. Which side of it somebody is born on shapes their income, their safety, and their opportunities more powerfully than almost any choice they will ever make. Since nobody selects their birthplace, this raises a genuine question of justice that the ordinary defence of borders rarely addresses. The standard defence appeals to self government. A political community makes decisions together, maintains institutions, and bears obligations to its members, and doing so requires knowing who belongs. Without some boundary the whole practice of collective self rule becomes unintelligible. This argument has real force, and it explains why even those troubled by borders rarely propose abolishing them. Yet the argument justifies less than it is usually asked to justify. It explains why a community may have members and rules; it does not explain why membership should be distributed by birth, which is the very kind of unchosen circumstance that moral thinking elsewhere refuses to treat as a ground of entitlement. A society that allocated positions internally by ancestry would be condemned immediately, and the international version differs only in scale. Two responses are available. One accepts the tension and holds that borders are justified pragmatically rather than morally, as a workable arrangement whose unfairness should be reduced wherever possible. The other argues that membership creates genuine obligations among members that outsiders cannot claim, so the inequality reflects a real moral difference rather than an arbitrary one. What neither response can honestly claim is that the current distribution is just. The most that can be defended is that borders serve valuable purposes while producing serious injustice, and that recognising both halves of that truth is the beginning of any useful argument about migration.

subject: 명예와 평판
title: Between what you are and what is said of you
content: Honour and reputation are frequently treated as one thing, and yet they come apart in ways that matter morally. Reputation is what others believe about somebody; honour, in the older sense, is a quality of the person themselves. A person may hold one without the other, and cultures differ enormously in which they emphasise. Where reputation dominates, the governing question is how conduct will appear. This has genuine advantages, since visible accountability restrains a great deal of wrongdoing that conscience alone would permit. It also has a characteristic failure: it rewards concealment as reliably as it rewards good conduct, so somebody skilled at managing appearances gains everything the honest person gains at considerably less cost. Where honour dominates, the governing question is what kind of person one is. This escapes the problem of concealment, because the standard is internal and cannot be satisfied by managing what others see. Yet it carries its own dangers, since honour codes have historically demanded violence over slights and have bound people to obligations that justice would reject. An internal standard is only as good as the standard internalised. The relation between the two is not simply opposition. Reputation supplies information, and a person's standing among those who know them well is evidence about their character, which is why we consult references and ask around. The failure occurs when reputation becomes the goal rather than the by-product, at which point the connection between the sign and the thing it signified is severed. What follows is a practical test that is easier to state than to pass. A person may ask whether they would do the same thing if nobody would ever learn of it, and the answer distinguishes the two orientations more reliably than any amount of reflection on one's own motives.

subject: 쾌락은 좋음의 척도인가
title: Whether pleasure measures what is good
content: One long tradition holds that pleasure is the only thing good in itself, and that everything else is valuable through its contribution to pleasure or its prevention of pain. The view is admirably clear, and it grounds a moral theory that requires no appeal to anything mysterious. Its difficulties emerge under pressure rather than at first sight. The first difficulty concerns kinds. Pleasures differ in more than quantity, and most people judge that some are worth more than others regardless of intensity or duration. Defenders of the tradition have tried to accommodate this by distinguishing higher from lower pleasures, although the distinction concedes that something other than pleasure is doing the ranking, which weakens the original claim considerably. A second difficulty concerns the object. Pleasure taken in another's suffering seems not merely unfortunate but worthless, and adding it to the total appears to make an outcome worse rather than better. If the theory must count such pleasure equally, its verdicts diverge sharply from every ordinary moral judgment. A third difficulty concerns what people actually pursue. Most of us want to accomplish things, to be loved rather than to feel loved, and to hold true beliefs, and these preferences persist even when we understand that the corresponding feeling could be produced more reliably by other means. That persistence is evidence that pleasure is not the whole of what we value. What survives the criticism is something narrower and still important. Pleasure and pain matter enormously, no account of the good life can ignore them, and theories that dismiss them as unworthy of philosophical attention have gone badly wrong in the opposite direction. The mistake lies in treating one genuine value as the single measure into which every other value must be converted.

subject: 아시리아 왕립 도서관의 점토판
title: The clay library of an ancient king
content: In the middle of the nineteenth century, excavators digging at Nineveh broke into rooms filled with broken clay. The fragments turned out to be tablets, tens of thousands of them, gathered by an Assyrian king in the seventh century before our era. It remains the largest surviving library from the ancient Near East, and its recovery reshaped what could be known about that world. The collection was assembled on purpose. Letters survive in which the king orders his agents to seek out texts in the temples and private houses of conquered cities and to send them to the capital, copying whatever cannot be taken. Consequently the shelves held not only records of the empire but works far older, some of them already ancient when they were copied. Among them was the fullest known version of a long poem about a king who searched for eternal life. The fire that destroyed the palace preserved the library. Clay left in the open crumbles, whereas clay that has been baked survives almost indefinitely, so the burning that ended the empire hardened the very tablets that recorded it. This accident of preservation explains why we know more about this civilization than about several of its neighbours whose archives were kept on materials that rot. Reading the collection took a century of work. The script had to be deciphered, the fragments matched, and pieces held in different museums rejoined, and that task continues today with the help of computers matching broken edges. What the tablets contain is remarkably varied: omens, medical recipes, word lists, astronomical observations, and letters from officials complaining about their colleagues. Taken together they show a civilization that valued the accumulation of written knowledge, and the king who gathered them understood that holding the texts of a conquered people was itself a form of rule.

subject: 이중 효과의 원리
title: Harm that comes with what you aimed at
content: Some actions produce a good result and a harmful one together, and a principle with a long history holds that such an action may be permissible under conditions that would forbid aiming at the harm directly. The doctrine appears in medical ethics, in the law of war, and in ordinary moral reasoning, and it deserves examination because it is invoked far more often than it is understood. The conditions are demanding. The act itself must not be wrong independently of its effects; the good result must be what the agent intends; the harm must not be the means by which the good is achieved; and the good must be proportionate to the harm allowed. Removing any of these conditions makes the principle permissive in ways nobody defends. The third condition does most of the work. Where the harm is the means, the agent has incorporated it into their plan, so that they would have to produce it again if it failed to occur. Where the harm is a side effect, the agent would welcome its absence. This is why bombing a factory and accepting civilian deaths differs morally from bombing civilians in order to break morale, although the totals may match. Critics attack the distinction from two directions. Some argue that it permits too much, since agents can redescribe their aims conveniently, and honest application depends on a self report that nobody can verify. Others argue that it forbids too little, since proportionality is elastic enough to justify almost anything. Both criticisms have merit, and the principle is genuinely easy to abuse. What defends it is the alternative. Without some such distinction, no difference remains between a surgeon whose patient dies and a killer whose victim dies, and moral thinking that cannot mark that difference has lost something essential.

subject: 신라 고분의 부장품
title: What was buried with the kings of Silla
content: The mounded tombs of the Silla kingdom stand in the middle of a modern city, grassed over and rounded, and for a long time nobody knew what lay inside. Their construction turned out to be the reason. Unlike chambered tombs that can be entered, these were built by placing a wooden chamber on the ground, heaping stones over it, and covering the whole with earth. Robbers could not tunnel in without the stones collapsing, therefore the contents survived intact for roughly fifteen centuries. What excavation revealed was extraordinary. Gold crowns with upright branching ornaments, belts hung with pendants, earrings of remarkable fineness, and vessels of glass appeared in numbers unmatched elsewhere in the region. The glass is particularly telling, since its composition points to workshops far to the west, which means this ancient kingdom sat at the end of a chain of exchange reaching across the continent. The crowns have been argued about for decades. Their branching uprights resemble trees and antlers, motifs associated with religious practice across the northern steppe, so many scholars read them as evidence of a shared tradition connecting the peninsula to peoples far to the north. Others emphasise local development. The debate matters because it bears on where this civilization understood itself to belong. The tombs also record change. Later burials contain fewer precious objects and different forms, which coincides with the arrival of a new religion that discouraged elaborate grave goods and encouraged cremation instead. Consequently the sequence of mounds preserves not only wealth but a shift in belief about what happens after death. What the excavations supply is a rare case where the archaeology is richer than the written record, since the histories of this era were composed centuries later and preserve almost nothing about how these people actually lived.

subject: 규칙 따르기와 예외
title: The person who thinks the rule does not apply to them
content: Everybody accepts that rules admit of exceptions, and everybody has met somebody who treats themselves as the standing exception. The difference between a justified departure and a self serving one is a genuine moral problem, made harder by the fact that both feel identical to the person making the judgment. Consider what the self serving version requires. The person does not reject the rule; they endorse it, and they believe others should follow it. What they claim is that their own case is special, usually because their reasons are unusually good or their circumstances unusually pressing. Since almost everybody believes their own reasons are good, this claim is available to anyone at any time, which is exactly why it cannot be accepted at face value. One useful test asks whether the exception could be stated publicly as a rule. If I would be willing to announce that anybody in my circumstances may do this, and to accept others doing it, then I am proposing a principled qualification rather than exempting myself. If the exception depends on remaining private, the reasoning has already failed. A second test asks who bears the cost. Rules typically exist because uncoordinated judgment produces bad results, therefore my departure imposes a cost on people relying on general compliance. Where I have not asked them and would not want them to know, the moral verdict is fairly clear. What makes this difficult in practice is that genuine exceptions exist, and a person too rigid to recognise them will do harm of a different kind. The honest position accepts that judgment is required while treating one's own convenience as evidence of bias rather than as a reason. Nobody applies that discipline perfectly, and the value of the tests lies in making the failure visible afterwards.

subject: 형벌의 비례성
title: Fitting the penalty to the offence
content: Nearly every legal tradition holds that a punishment should be proportionate to the offence, and the principle is invoked as though its meaning were obvious. It is not. Proportionality requires ranking offences by seriousness and penalties by severity, and then matching the two scales, and each of those steps involves judgments that are far from settled. Ranking offences is the more tractable half. Most people agree that violence is worse than theft and that deliberate wrongdoing is worse than negligence, so a rough order can be established. Difficulties appear at the margins, particularly for offences whose harm is diffuse, since damaging thousands of people slightly may be worse in total than injuring one person seriously while feeling considerably less grave. Ranking penalties is harder than it appears. A fine that is trivial for one person may be ruinous for another, therefore identical penalties are not equally severe, and systems that ignore this impose unequal punishment while claiming to treat people alike. Imprisonment raises the same problem, since its effect depends on age, health, and what a person had to lose. Matching the scales is hardest of all. Nothing in the nature of an offence indicates how many years it deserves, and the numbers used by any legal system are inherited rather than derived. Comparison across countries makes this plain: the same act attracts sentences differing by an order of magnitude, and each society regards its own scale as obviously correct. What proportionality can deliver, despite these problems, is internal consistency. Even without knowing the right absolute penalty, a system can ensure that worse offences receive heavier punishment than lesser ones, and that similar cases are treated similarly. Justice of that limited kind is worth having, and many systems fail to achieve even this.

subject: 흙둔덕 문화의 의례 공간
title: Earth raised into shapes across a continent
content: Across the river valleys of eastern North America stand thousands of mounds built of heaped earth. Some are conical, some flat topped and terraced, and a few are shaped as animals stretching hundreds of feet across the ground. They were raised by many different peoples across roughly four thousand years, and taken together they represent one of the great building traditions of the ancient world. The earliest examples predate agriculture in the region, which upset an assumption that long shaped archaeology. Large scale construction was thought to require farming, since only a settled surplus could support the labour, and yet these mounds were built by people who fished, hunted, and gathered. The ancient builders assembled in numbers and worked without any of the conditions the theory demanded. Later centuries produced sites of considerable scale. One centre near the Mississippi held a mound covering more ground at its base than the largest Egyptian pyramid, along with plazas, smaller platforms, and a surrounding city that may have housed twenty thousand people. Its rise and decline occupied only a few centuries, and the reasons for both are still argued about. The purposes varied. Some mounds covered burials, some supported buildings, and some appear to have marked ground for gatherings rather than serving any structural role. The animal shapes are the hardest to explain, since they are best appreciated from a height that nobody could reach, and the most credible readings connect them to ritual movement along their outlines. Much has been lost. Nineteenth century settlers ploughed most of these earthworks flat, and a persistent story attributed them to a vanished race rather than to the ancestors of the peoples who lived there. That story was disproved long ago, although the destruction it excused cannot be undone.

subject: 아름다움의 객관성
title: Whether beauty is in the object at all
content: When somebody calls a thing beautiful, they seem to describe it rather than themselves. The grammar suggests a property, and yet no examination of the object reveals anything corresponding to that property in the way examination reveals its mass or colour. This gap has driven a long philosophical argument about what such judgments actually claim. The subjective position holds that beauty names a response. Certain arrangements produce a characteristic pleasure in observers, and calling something beautiful reports that response rather than any feature of the thing. On this view disagreements are not genuine, since each person reports accurately about themselves, and the appearance of conflict comes from a misleading grammar. Against this stands the persistence of argument. People who disagree about a work do not behave as though they were reporting different sensations; they offer reasons, point at features, and sometimes change their minds. That pattern is characteristic of disputes about truth rather than about taste, and any adequate theory must explain why the practice takes this shape. A middle position holds that beauty depends upon both. The response is genuinely in the observer, and yet it is a response to something, so a judgment can be better or worse according to how much of the object it takes in. Somebody who has learned a tradition perceives relations that a newcomer cannot, therefore their pleasure rests on more of what is there. This is not objectivity of the kind physics supplies, although it is enough to make training worthwhile. What the debate finally illuminates is why aesthetic education exists at all. If beauty were purely a matter of individual response, there would be nothing to teach, and yet the entire history of art criticism consists of people showing each other what to look at. The practice is evidence that the middle position is roughly right.

subject: 고원 농업의 융기밭
title: Raised fields on a cold high plain
content: On the plain surrounding a great lake in the Andes, at an altitude where frost threatens crops through much of the year, ancient farmers built raised beds separated by water channels. The pattern covers enormous areas, and for centuries it lay abandoned and unrecognised, visible mainly as ridges under the grass. Aerial survey revealed the extent, and excavation established the age. The design solves the central problem of the place. Water in the channels absorbs heat during the day and releases it at night, so the air just above the beds stays several degrees warmer than the surrounding plain. That margin is the difference between a harvest and a failure, therefore the ancient builders had engineered a defence against the one hazard that made farming there uncertain. The channels served other purposes as well. Silt and plant material accumulating in them could be lifted onto the beds as fertiliser, and the water supported fish and aquatic plants that supplemented the diet. Consequently the system produced more than a crop, and estimates of its yield suggest it could support a substantial population on ground that later generations regarded as marginal. This capacity underwrote the civilization centred on the lake. Its ceremonial city, built of precisely fitted stone, drew on the surplus these fields produced, and the political reach of that centre extended across a wide territory during several centuries of the first millennium. When the centre declined, the fields fell out of use. What makes this case unusual is that the archaeology has been tested. Experimental plots rebuilt on the ancient pattern in recent decades produced harvests substantially exceeding those of modern methods on the same ground, which confirms the interpretation and demonstrates that ancient technique is not automatically inferior to what replaced it.

subject: 도덕적 진보는 있는가
title: Whether morality gets better over time
content: We speak confidently of moral progress, pointing to the abolition of slavery, the extension of the vote, and the recognition of rights once denied. Yet the claim is philosophically awkward, since judging that later views are better requires a standard, and using our own standard makes the conclusion automatic. Every generation has believed itself an improvement on the last. One response denies that any external standard is needed. Progress can be identified by internal criteria: a moral view improves when it becomes more consistent, when it rests on fewer false factual beliefs, and when it can be defended to those it affects. Slavery failed all three tests, and its defenders relied on claims about human difference that turned out to be false. On this reading the advance is genuine and demonstrable. A second response points to whose judgment is being consulted. The people subjected to a practice have rarely regarded it as acceptable, so the appearance that standards merely changed reflects whose views were recorded rather than whether anybody objected. Recognising a wrong is frequently a matter of listening to testimony that was always available. Against these arguments stands the observation that progress is neither steady nor guaranteed. Societies have moved backward, cruelties have been reinvented, and the technical capacity for harm has grown faster than the restraint on using it. Anybody who treats improvement as automatic is reading a selected portion of the record. What can be defended is a modest claim. Moral change is not merely change, since some views survive scrutiny better than others, and the direction of travel over long periods has been toward including people previously excluded. That trend is real, it was produced by argument and struggle rather than by time, and nothing whatever guarantees that it continues.

subject: 결과가 판단을 바꿔도 되는가
title: Judging a decision by how it turned out
content: A decision that produced disaster invites condemnation, and one that produced success invites praise. Yet the quality of a decision must be assessed by what the decider knew and how they reasoned, since the outcome frequently depends on factors nobody could control. Judging by results therefore looks like a mistake, and it is a mistake that almost everybody makes. The error has a familiar shape. Once an outcome is known, it becomes difficult to recover the uncertainty that existed beforehand, and the path that actually occurred seems to have been visible all along. Consequently a reasonable gamble that failed is remembered as reckless, while an unreasonable one that succeeded is remembered as bold, and the moral verdicts follow the memory rather than the reasoning. Yet the opposite position also fails. If outcomes were entirely irrelevant, then a person who took a serious risk with other people's welfare would be blameless whenever they were lucky, and that conclusion is hard to accept. Somebody who drove dangerously and hit nobody did something wrong, and something worse happens when they hit somebody, even though the driving was identical. Our practices track both facts. A workable position separates the questions. Assessing the reasoning asks what the person knew and whether they weighed it properly, and that assessment should ignore the outcome entirely. Assessing what is now owed asks about the harm actually caused, and that assessment cannot ignore it. Both are legitimate, and confusing them produces the familiar injustice in which a careful person is condemned for bad luck. The practical value lies in institutional design. Reviews conducted after a failure should ask what information was available at the time, because a process that punishes outcomes rather than reasoning teaches people to avoid records rather than to think better.

subject: 말리 제국의 순례 여정
title: The journey that told the world about an empire
content: In the fourteenth century a ruler of the Mali empire crossed the Sahara on pilgrimage to Mecca, and the journey entered the historical record of three continents. Accounts written in Egypt describe a caravan of thousands, camels loaded with gold, and a procession that halted the ordinary business of Cairo for months. The visit is among the best documented moments in the medieval history of west Africa. The gold is the detail that everyone repeats. Chroniclers report that the king distributed and spent so much of it in Egypt that its value there fell and did not recover for years, which if approximately true makes this the clearest surviving demonstration of the wealth that the trans-Saharan routes carried. The metal came from fields to the south of the empire, and control of the routes rather than of the mines was the basis of the state's power. The journey had consequences beyond spectacle. European mapmakers, working from Arabic accounts, began placing the empire and its ruler on their charts, and a famous atlas of the following century depicts him enthroned holding a golden orb. Consequently a civilization that Europeans had never visited acquired a definite place in their picture of the world, drawn entirely from testimony carried along trading networks. The ruler also brought scholars and architects home with him. Building programmes in the cities of the middle Niger followed, and the libraries assembled there over subsequent centuries preserved manuscripts that survive today. What the pilgrimage records, therefore, is not merely wealth but a state confident enough to spend a year away from its capital. The empire declined within two centuries, and later European accounts of the region forgot almost everything these sources had established, which is a reminder that historical knowledge can be lost as well as gained.

subject: 무고한 사람을 쓰는 일
title: Using somebody who did nothing wrong
content: Some of the hardest cases in moral philosophy involve harming an innocent person in order to prevent a much greater harm. What makes them hard is not the arithmetic, which is usually plain, but a conviction that certain things may not be done to people regardless of what follows. Understanding that conviction is central to the argument between competing theories. One tradition treats the conviction as a rule of thumb that occasionally misfires. Rules against using people exist because such conduct usually produces bad results, and where the numbers are extreme the rule should yield. Refusing to act, on this view, prefers the cleanliness of one's own record to the lives of many, which is a form of self indulgence rather than a moral achievement. The opposing tradition treats the conviction as tracking something the arithmetic omits. A person used as an instrument is not merely harmed; they are treated as material for other people's purposes, and no explanation could be offered to them that they could reasonably accept. Justice on this view concerns what can be justified to each individual rather than what maximises across a group. A subtler consideration concerns what a permission would do. A rule allowing innocents to be used whenever the numbers favour it would make everyone's security conditional on continuous calculation by others, and the value of not being available for such use is itself considerable. This is an argument the first tradition can partly accept, since the effects of the permission are themselves consequences. What the debate does not permit is confident dismissal of either side. Most people hold both convictions, refusing to use one person to save five while accepting some sacrifices for greater numbers, and no theory yet proposed reconciles those judgments without discarding one of them.

subject: 로마 국경 방벽의 유적
title: What a frontier wall was actually for
content: Stone walls, ditches, and forts mark the northern edge of what was once Roman territory, running across northern Britain and along the rivers of central Europe. They are usually described as defences against invasion, and that description turns out to be only partly right. Excavation across the past century has produced a more interesting account of what these ancient works accomplished. The physical evidence resists a purely military reading. Gateways occur at regular intervals, in some sectors every mile, which would be a strange design for a barrier meant to stop an army. The wall in Britain is thick and tall enough to require enormous labour and yet has no continuous fighting platform of the kind a defensive work needs. Its towers are placed for observation rather than for concentrated shooting. A better explanation treats the line as a controlled boundary. Traffic could be channelled through the gates, taxed, counted, and inspected, and small raiding parties driving stolen livestock could be stopped where a full army could not. The garrison also gained a platform for patrolling well beyond the wall itself, since forts north of the line were occupied throughout much of the period. There is a further purpose that the stones announce plainly. A structure of this scale, visible for miles, declares that the empire ends here by decision rather than by exhaustion, and the labour invested was itself a statement to anybody watching from either side. Roman writers of the era describe such works in exactly those terms. The later history complicates the picture. Sections were abandoned, reoccupied, and rebuilt as the frontier moved, and the archaeology shows long stretches of peaceful exchange across the line. What the ruins record is therefore a relationship rather than a siege, maintained for roughly three centuries by an empire that had decided where to stop.

subject: 착취란 무엇인가
title: When a bargain is unfair rather than merely hard
content: Both parties to an exchange may agree, both may gain, and the arrangement may still be exploitative. This possibility puzzles theories that treat consent as sufficient, since the person exploited chose the arrangement and was made better off by it. Explaining what goes wrong requires looking beyond whether an agreement occurred. The clearest cases involve unequal vulnerability. Somebody desperate for work, medicine, or shelter will accept terms that nobody with alternatives would consider, and the party offering those terms is taking advantage of a weakness they did not create. What makes the transaction troubling is that the gain to the stronger party comes precisely from the other's lack of options. This suggests that exploitation concerns the distribution of the benefit rather than the fact of consent. Cooperation between two parties usually produces a surplus, and the question is how that surplus is divided. Where one side captures nearly all of it because the other cannot walk away, the arrangement is unfair even though both are better off than they would have been alone. Two complications deserve attention. First, refusing to deal with somebody desperate leaves them worse off, so condemning the exploiter does not by itself help the exploited, and prohibitions occasionally remove the only option available. Second, judging the fair division requires a standard, and reasonable people disagree about what a fair share of a jointly produced surplus looks like. Neither complication dissolves the concept. What they establish is that the moral response cannot stop at criticising individual bargains, since the underlying problem is the vulnerability that made the terms possible. Justice here points toward changing the conditions under which people negotiate rather than merely condemning those who exploit them, although both responses have their place.

subject: 판화의 복수성과 원본 개념
title: An art made to exist many times
content: Most visual art produces a single object, and its value is bound to that uniqueness. Printmaking works differently, since the artist creates a matrix — a carved block, an incised plate, a prepared stone — and the image itself appears only when the matrix is inked and pressed. Every impression is equally the work, which unsettles the whole idea of an original. This has practical consequences that shaped the tradition. Printmakers number their impressions and limit the edition, not because later impressions are inferior in principle but because the matrix wears, and a plate that has produced two hundred sheets no longer holds the fine lines it began with. The convention therefore records a physical fact while also protecting the market, and separating those two motives is not always possible. The medium's reproducibility determined its cultural role. Prints travelled where paintings could not, carrying compositions across borders and making the work of distant artists available to anybody who could afford a sheet. Much of what European artists knew of each other's work before photography they knew through engravings, so the history of style is partly a history of what happened to be printed. Reproductive prints also altered the originals, since the copyist's choices about tone and emphasis became how the painting was known. The aesthetic possibilities are specific to each technique. A woodcut carries the resistance of the block in its bold line, an etching records the freedom of a needle moving through soft ground, and a lithograph preserves the character of a drawn mark. Consequently the medium is not merely a way of multiplying an image but a family of distinct artistic languages, and printmakers have generally understood their work as invention rather than as reproduction, whatever the market has believed.

subject: 초상화가 감춘 신분의 표지
title: Reading rank in a painted face
content: A portrait appears to record a face, and yet almost everything else in the picture is doing work. Clothing, posture, background, and the objects placed near the sitter all carry information that contemporaries read without effort and that later viewers miss entirely. Learning to see these signals turns a gallery of faces into a document about how a culture ranked its members. Fabric is the most reliable indicator. Certain dyes were extremely costly, particular weaves were restricted by law in some societies, and the sheer quantity of cloth in a garment announced how much could be afforded. A painter rendered these details with care because the sitter was paying for exactly that recognition, therefore the technical brilliance of the drapery is itself part of the message rather than mere display of skill. Objects supply a second layer. A book indicates learning, a globe or an instrument indicates the reach of trade or the pursuit of knowledge, and a dog at the feet has meant fidelity in a long tradition of European painting. Such items were rarely present at the sitting; they were chosen for the composition, so the picture presents an argument about the sitter rather than a record of a room. Posture and scale complete the design. A figure occupying the full height of a large canvas, seen from slightly below, claims something that a modest half length cannot. Group portraits encode relative standing through position, height, and who looks at whom, and disputes about these arrangements are recorded in the contracts. What follows for anybody looking at such work is that the face is frequently the least informative part. The tradition was producing statements about position within a social order, and reading them requires knowing the vocabulary that the original audience absorbed without ever being taught.

subject: 혐오 표현을 규제하는 논거
title: The case for and against restricting hateful speech
content: Few disputes about liberty are conducted with less patience than this one. Defenders of restriction describe their opponents as indifferent to harm, and opponents describe defenders as authoritarian, and both descriptions occasionally fit. Setting the moral arguments out plainly is more useful than either accusation. The case for restriction begins with effects on standing. Speech directed at a group as a group does not merely offend; it asserts that its members are appropriately treated as lesser, and where such assertions are common they change how those people are actually treated. The harm is therefore not hurt feelings but a degradation of civic standing, which is a matter of justice rather than of comfort. A second argument concerns participation, since people who are targeted persistently withdraw from public discussion, so the restriction defended is presented as protecting speech overall. The case against begins with the difficulty of drawing the line. Any authority empowered to identify unacceptable speech will use that power according to its own interests, and the historical record of such powers is not encouraging. Laws written to protect vulnerable groups have been applied against them, since those groups frequently lack the influence to control enforcement. A second argument holds that suppression drives beliefs out of view without changing them, removing the opportunity to answer them openly. What both sides share, once the accusations are set aside, is a concern for the standing of vulnerable people. They disagree about whether legal restriction improves that standing or endangers it, which is partly an empirical question about how such laws actually operate. Treating it as an empirical question rather than a test of moral character would improve the argument considerably, since the evidence from different countries is genuinely mixed and neither side's confidence is warranted by it.

subject: 풍경화가 발명한 자연
title: How painting taught people to see the countryside
content: Landscape appears in European painting for centuries as background, filling the space behind figures whose story the picture told. Its emergence as a subject in its own right happened comparatively late, and the change involved more than a shift in taste. A culture had to decide that the countryside was worth looking at, and painting was among the instruments by which it decided. The earlier attitude is easily forgotten. Mountains were obstacles, forests were dangerous, and cultivated ground was valued for its yield rather than its appearance. Travellers crossing the Alps in earlier centuries recorded discomfort rather than admiration, so the aesthetic response that now seems natural had to be learned. Painters, poets, and eventually tourists learned it together, and the sequence in which they did so is traceable. Certain conventions did the teaching. Painters composed views with a dark framing element at the edge, a lit middle distance, and a receding blue horizon, and this arrangement made a stretch of country legible as a picture. Travellers then carried tinted glasses designed to reproduce the tonal effect, turning to look at the view over their shoulder in a mirror so that it resembled the paintings they admired. The art had supplied the standard against which actual scenery was judged. Consequently the countryside that visitors sought out was the countryside that resembled the tradition. Regions matching the convention became destinations, and estates were reshaped to look like the paintings their owners collected, with clumped trees and irregular water replacing formal geometry. What the whole episode demonstrates is how completely an aesthetic tradition can construct a response that feels immediate. Nobody standing before a wide view experiences the pleasure as learned, and yet the terms in which it is felt were assembled by particular artists working in a particular period.

subject: 합창 전통과 공동체의 목소리
title: Singing together and what it makes
content: Group singing exists in nearly every culture, and its persistence is worth explaining, since it is not obviously useful. A community that sings together produces no goods and gains no direct advantage, and yet the practice appears in worship, in labour, in mourning, and in celebration across traditions with no contact between them. Part of the answer lies in what the activity requires. Singing in a group demands continuous adjustment: each voice must listen to the others, match pitch, and align rhythm, so the practice trains exactly the kind of mutual attention that cooperation depends upon. Participants report a distinctive feeling of merging with the group, and the physical mechanism is real, since breathing synchronises among singers holding a shared line. The musical traditions themselves record different ideas about the collective. Some cultures cultivate a blended sound in which individual voices become indistinguishable, which expresses one understanding of what a community is. Others prize a texture in which each singer remains audible, weaving independent lines, and that difference in aesthetic preference corresponds to a difference in how the group imagines itself. Neither is more natural; both are cultivated. The social function extends beyond the moment of performance. A tradition of songs carries texts across generations, and in societies without writing this was among the principal means by which history, law, and genealogy were preserved. Melody assists memory, and the requirement to sing together keeps the version consistent, since a soloist may drift while a group corrects itself. What the practice finally offers is a form of participation that is available to almost everyone and that produces something nobody could produce alone. Cultures that have industrialised their music, turning most people into listeners, have lost something specific, and the persistence of amateur choirs suggests that the loss is felt.
